whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text:
Hi, my name is Ed Baer. I look like this.
And I'm presenting a new piece called 9 Degrees of Freedom
that you can see in the background strobing behind me,
which is nine separate video projectors in a color-mixing stroboscopic array
such that every mix of three projections results in white light,
though each projector is never projecting white light,
spread in a kind of spatial parallax so that as you move through the space
and cast shadow in the projection,
you basically break down the natural color-mixing,
space- and time-based color-mixing that your eyes do into their component parts.
And really the idea behind this
is only to make it look like a
really two-fold.
One is I wanted to make a space that's really fun to play in,
that has a bit of like an activated interactive feel,
but without extra layers of technology,
just something built into the way that video works,
that explains how video works to your eye,
without a lot of sensors or anything,
just a trick of light that's fun to play with.
Also kind of a side effect of this that I was really interested in
is how different the perception of light is
versus how we would record it.
In our world, the moment that something gets interesting,
someone pulls out a phone or a camera
and starts to document themselves in the space,
and because of the stroboscopic action of this piece,
what you document is completely different than your live experience.
Like what the camera sees,
because it mixes color and time differently than our eyes does,
is very, very different.
And it's not better or worse,
but it's not better.
Or worse, it just calls attention to that fact
that the way that video is working on our perceptual systems
is very different than what's happening in the millisecond
and inside of the text image.
Really the source video for the piece is just single color fields,
just blocks of light.
Sometimes it's subtractive color mixing,
sometimes it's additive color mixing,
meaning that those color fields are red, green, or blue.
Sometimes I'm mixing those,
a kind of complementary color wheel,
and that's the visual effect.
But there's always three colors overlaying one another
that mix down to white.
